utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is case number IT-99-36-PT, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner on behalf of the Prosecutor, together with Anna Richterova and Adele Erasmus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman, and I appear here on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. And for Mr. Talic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Your microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DE ROUX
utterances.text: I'm Xavier de Roux acting for Mr. Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. De Roux.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Michel Pitron, counsel for Mr. Talic. And Ms. Natasha is with us this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pitron. Now, the first matter we have to deal with is the application by Mr. Brdjanin for provisional release. Mr. Ackerman, the Prosecution has said that they did not wish to cross-examine your witness if the evidence was limited to the statement that he'd made, but we said you may bring him if you wish. Have you brought him?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He's here, Your Honour. I understood that it wasn't a "may bring him if I wished" but an order from the Court that he needed to be here, and so that's why he's here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. I very clearly said that he may come if he wish, and if he does, he will be cross-examined if he gives evidence outside his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I obviously somehow misunderstood that, Your Honour, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Let me just read it to you just so that there can be no doubt about it. "I hereby order that the order on additional witness statement is varied so that Milan Trbojevic" -- how does he pronounce his name?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. "... is not required to attend the oral hearing, but if he does attend the hearing for the purpose of giving evidence in relation to the provisional release motion, he may be cross-examined in relation to any evidence given which relates to subject matter going beyond that contained in the witness statement."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he's here and I would like to put him on the witness stand, since he's gone to all the trouble to get here, and I will do it as briefly as I possibly can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well, then. You call your witness, then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure where he is, but Victims and Witnesses told me that he would be here at this moment so I assume that he is. Milan Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Would you please take the solemn oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please sit down, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Honourable Tribunal who you are?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Milan Trbojevic. I have a degree in law; I was a judge for many years and a lawyer in Sarajevo. Recently, I was Minister of Justice in the government of Republika Srpska until the end of March this year, and now I hold the post of Advisor to the Prime Minister of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where do you live?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: In Banja Luka, in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know my client, Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How long have you known Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we met perhaps in 1991, in Sarajevo, when the National Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina was convening. Before the war, we were both MPs. Since then we have been seeing each other quite often, and later we even worked together closely as Ministers in the government of Republika Srpska. We were MPs in the Assembly of Republika Srpska until the summer of 1994, when first he and then four of us MPs were dismissed from that Assembly. Then as citizens of Banja Luka, we would see each other. In January 1996, that is to say, soon after the Dayton Peace Agreement was signed, Mr. Brdjanin and I established a political party together. We called it the People's Party of Republika Srpska. We wanted to join the new developments in Republika Srpska, and this was not an easy thing. I was excluded from this party sometime -- well, I don't know exactly -- in 1997 or the beginning of 1998. I'm not quite sure about that now. After that we did see each other a few times in town, just like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your acquaintance with Mr. Brdjanin, could it be described as something more than just a casual acquaintance, that you know him reasonably well and that you've established a kind of friendship with him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this acquaintance has been there for about ten years, and I think I know him quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Based upon that, I want to ask you a brief series of questions. Based upon your knowledge and acquaintanceship with Mr. Brdjanin, can you tell the Tribunal whether or not you believe he would harass, intimidate, or otherwise interfere with any persons who are or may be witnesses for the Prosecutor in the case against him, either directly or indirectly? Do you believe he would or would not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm quite sure that he would not. I know him as an exceptional man, as a man who keeps his word. Whenever he makes a promise, whenever he gives his word, whenever he says he will do something, he indeed honours what he says and the obligations he takes upon himself. So I can answer that question with certainty. I'm convinced that he would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Based again upon your knowledge and acquaintance with Mr. Brdjanin, do you believe that he would report to the Tribunal here in The Hague on every occasion the Tribunal asked him to do so?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what I have said just now, I'm sure that he would. I had the opportunity of talking to him before the government of Republika Srpska gave a guarantee for him, that is to say, that his presence before this Court would have to be ensured even if he did not respond himself. And he assured me that there was no dilemma whatsoever, he would, indeed -- he'd keep his promise to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In that connection, in your discussion with him about the government issuing a guarantee to this Tribunal, did you explain to him in any way that he needed to understand that if the government issued such a guarantee that it would absolutely enforce that guarantee?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: We discussed the guarantee in detail, its terms and conditions, and also the obligation that it had to be honoured.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Based upon your knowledge and acceptance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Ackerman, it's not clear to me with whom he discussed. With your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll make that very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, it's my understanding, and correct me if I'm wrong, that on each occasion that a detainee has requested such a guarantee from your government, that some representative of the government has met with that detainee regarding that matter and in that process has explained to the detainee that the government would intend to absolutely enforce the terms of their guarantee; is that a true statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly the way it's been. In addition to what the liaison officer discussed with all the detainees, including Mr. Brdjanin, I had the opportunity of talking to him when the Prime Minister of Republika Srpska visited about a month or a month and a half ago. When we visited the detainees here, we talked to all, almost everybody, including Mr. Brdjanin. So that is the kind of discussion that was held, in that spirit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you one further question on a previous matter and then I'll have another question about the guarantee process. Based upon your knowledge and acquaintanceship with Mr. Brdjanin, do you believe that he would report to the police or other authorities in Banja Luka whenever the Court might direct that he do so?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I, indeed, believe that without any reservation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: From what you've just told us about the issuance of guarantees by the government of Republika Srpska, I gather that in your capacity as Minister of Justice, that you played some role in establishing the government's policy with regard to those guarantees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: While I was Minister, in a significant measure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's my understanding that the government's policy with regard to those guarantees is to view them not only as a representation to the Tribunal but as an understanding between the government and the detainee that the guarantees will be strictly and absolutely enforced and that they're not issued without that understanding between the government and the detainee himself; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is the position of the Prime Minister for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trbojevic. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, do you know what Mr. Brdjanin is charged with?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did see the first indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you appreciate that Mr. Brdjanin is charged with genocide, amongst other offences.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I read everything that the indictment says.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You tell us that you have no doubt that he will abide by the conditions that this Tribunal may impose.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If he failed to report to the police station, how would you know about it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm still an official in the government of Republika Srpska and I sit relatively close to the Minister of Police, and I'm even closer to the Prime Minister, so I would know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What would you do about it? What could you do about it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I could ask the Minister of Police to do his part of the job.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you proposing to live with Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean by "with"?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In his house.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I have a family of my own.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't see how I could integrate these two families now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So if he decided to leave the country, you would only know about it if the police chief reported it to you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If he attempted to get in touch with a witness, you would only know about it if the witness complained to the police and the police told you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: None, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may leave now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is that all the evidence, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's it, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any evidence in reply, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman, it's your motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, very largely the matters I would wish to bring to the attention of the Trial Chamber I have done so in my written submissions to you. You have before you not only the testimony of Mr. Trbojevic, but you have before you the statement of Mrs. Brdjanin that the Prosecution has accepted without the necessity of cross-examination. By saying that, I'm not saying the Prosecution agrees with the statement but only that it's been accepted without cross-examination. You have before you the personal guarantee of Mr. Brdjanin himself, and you have before you the guarantee of the government of Republika Srpska that we've just heard some testimony about. I think it's revealing and helpful to Mr. Brdjanin's position to understand the position that the government takes with regard to those guarantees, and that is that they are not just representations made to the Tribunal but undertakings between the government and a detainee that if the detainee wants the government to issue such a guarantee, that detainee must understand that it will be vigorously enforced and complied with. There are really only two issues according to Rule 65 that need to be established: one, that the accused will appear for trial if released and, second, that he will not pose a danger to any victim, witness, or other person. With regard to that, let me say this: When the Plenary decided to modify Rule 65 by removing "there from the requirement that the detainee establish additional circumstances to justify relief," the approach to the process of provisional release was rather dramatically changed, I believe. And what we have done with our presentation is we have presented evidence that Mr. Brdjanin will appear for trial and will not pose a danger to any victim, witness, or other person. The Prosecutor largely responds with a yes, but he's charged with genocide and crimes against humanity. Paraphrasing an order of this Chamber entered just recently, when the Plenary decided to modify Rule 65 by removing the exceptional circumstances language from it, the Chamber was fully aware that that Rule applies to every detainee at this Tribunal including those charged with genocide and crimes against humanity. The Plenary did not seek to accept those particular offences from the provisions regarding provisional release. And as this Chamber has held in another context, a prevailing circumstance can never be an exceptional circumstance, and the prevailing circumstance, when the Plenary modified Rule 65, was that some detainees were charged with genocide and crimes against humanity. So it seems to me that that is not an exceptional circumstance the Prosecutor can rely on as a basis not to grant a provisional release. Finally, and just very briefly, the Prosecution has also contended in one of their responses that my position regarding the nature of the change in Rule 65 is largely incorrect and that it was not the intention of the Plenary to remove the exceptional circumstances language in a sense that would make provisional release the presumption rather than an unusual situation, and I think that's exactly what the Plenary had in mind, to try to bring the Rules of this Tribunal in line with other international documents regarding the release of persons awaiting trial. There is support for that now in the Appeals Chamber decision in the Simic case on the application for provisional release where that issue was raised by the Prosecution and their efforts to appeal that concept were rejected by the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That was really a very different point. What they were trying to argue there was that the Rule as amended was ultra vires. I think they've dropped that rather strange argument. They certainly haven't repeated it in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In any event, I think it's quite clear that the Plenary was trying to bring the Tribunal in line with other international instruments when they made this change to the Rule. And it seems to me that the situation that the Tribunal faces now under this new Rule is that there is some obligation on the Prosecutor, there's a burden on the Prosecutor, if you will, to show that there are exceptional circumstances in a particular case that militate against provisional release, that go beyond what I would describe as the prevailing circumstances in all the cases. And I think the Prosecution has failed to do so, and I would strongly urge this Chamber to grant our motion for provisional release. And with that, I will conclude my remarks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I deal, first of all, with Mr. Ackerman's final submission, that the burden is now on the Prosecution to show that there are exceptional circumstances justifying the detention of an accused. With respect, we disagree with Mr. Ackerman's submissions on this. When one looks at Rule 65, it still reads: "Provisional release, once detained, an accused may not be released except upon the order of a Trial Chamber." We submit that it's still the onus on the accused to show why release should be ordered once the Trial Chamber has ordered his detention. We accept, of course, that the phrase "exceptional circumstances" have gone but the Trial Chamber still has to be satisfied, we submit, by the accused that he will appear for trial and if released will not pose a danger to any victim, witness, or other person. Your Honour, of course we've mentioned the fact of genocide because it's the most serious offence that can be charged in this Tribunal. There is, therefore, a real risk because of the likely sentence, if there is a conviction, that if released this accused will decide that the risk is too great and not appear for trial. The application is for the accused, Radoslav Brdjanin, to be released back into Banja Luka in the Republika Srpska. This Tribunal has no control at all over any part of Bosnia but, we submit, the least control or the least influence in the Republika Srpska. This Tribunal has no police force by which it can enforce the conditions of release or cause an arrest to be made if those conditions are breached. With the greatest of respect, the Republika Srpska, despite its many assertions in writing and orally, has so far declined to cooperate in any way with this Tribunal in respect of the arrest or detention of people who have been indicted. And we regret to say that the guarantee provided by the Republika Srpska, that should Mr. Brdjanin breach any conditions they will arrest him, should be treated in the light of past events with a great deal of caution. Your Honour, there's a further risk, and that deals with the danger to any victim, witness, or other person. Your Honours have ordered that the Prosecution release the identities of the witnesses who have already been disclosed to the Defence and in future, any further witnesses that we wish to disclose to them unless there are good reasons which will be provided for in a motion to Your Honours. Your Honour, the area of Banja Luka is the area in which these crimes, or part of the area in which these crimes which are alleged are said to have occurred. There are witnesses or potential witnesses who will be disclosed who reside within that area. If Mr. Brdjanin were to be released in that area, he is free, whatever may be said by his acquaintance, to take such measures as he wishes in respect of those witnesses. The names which will be disclosed to him, plus the identities, will be available to him. We submit that the burden does lie upon Mr. Brdjanin to show that it would be safe and proper to release him and that what Your Honours have heard today does not satisfy that burden, and that the risk that he will fail to appear for trial and/or interfere with witnesses is a real and substantial one, and we invite Your Honours to dismiss this application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Anything in reply, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. First of all, it's a very creative reading of Rule 65(A) that it somehow says that the Prosecution has no burden and the entire burden is upon the Defence. 65(A) reads: "An accused may not be released except upon an order of a Trial Chamber." To me what that means is that the Prosecutor or the Defence lawyer or the Registrar can't order his release, only the Trial Chamber can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think you are right. But if you look at paragraph (B), it puts it a little more firmly. "The Trial Chamber has to be satisfied that the accused will appear for trial and will not pose a danger." That clearly puts the onus on you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, and I think we've carried that burden. Then it shifts to the Prosecution to, I think, show any exceptional circumstances to the contrary. That's the way I see it. I remain convinced that the Prosecution has failed to do so. All the Prosecution has done is tell you that he is charged with genocide. They have told you that there is a risk of flight and a risk that he will interfere with witnesses. But they've simply done that in the form of Ms. Korner's opinion as a totally subjective statement. There's nothing objectively presented to you that could possibly lead you to the conclusion that there is a danger that he will do either of those things. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. With regard to risk of flight, as you know from the documents submitted, Mr. Brdjanin has a wife and two daughters who live in Banja Luka. While he has been detained here, they have visited him frequently. He is very close to that family. Mr. Brdjanin would not want to put himself in a position by being released where he would not be able to continue that relationship with his family, and his family certainly is not going to uproot themselves and go live in the mountains or anything like that. So I think there is largely no chance whatsoever that Mr. Brdjanin is going to not simply go back to Banja Luka and continue living in his government flat as he has for the last several years. His wife has a job in Banja Luka. I would except Mr. Brdjanin to return to work in Banja Luka and help support his family. And he really has no reason not to live up to that which the Tribunal asks him to do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Trial Chamber will reserve its decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: 11.35 a.m., to be followed by a Status Conference

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Motion Hearing adjourned at
